In 'towards calm and insight', what is the primary Dhamma theme and practical guidance offered?

In 'towards calm and insight', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Pothgulgala Dharmagrantha 
Dharmasravana Màdhya Bhàraya
 This is to inform our readers that all Dhamma 
books so far written and yet to be written by  
Venerable Bhikkhu Katukurunde ¥àõananda will 
hereafter be published by the P.D.D.M.B."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as an external philosophy, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text emphasizes, the Dhamma is *akāliko* (timeless) and *opanayiko* (leading inward), realizable (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner through patient, honest awareness.

In 'towards calm and insight', anicca is discussed in this context: *"Why 

anicca and dukkha and the word dhamma is introduced with 
reference to anattà?"* Here, anicca (impermanence (anicca)) is treated not as a theoretical doctrine, but as a living faculty to be actively cultivated and observed. When we bring genuine mindfulness to our direct experience, the quality of anicca helps dismantle habitual delusion and stabilizes the mind in clear, unentangled awareness.

In 'towards calm and insight', how are we advised to handle suffering (dukkha) and emotional stress?

The text teaches: *"A cessation of 
personality (sakkàyanirodho) which is not tantamount to 
annihilation will appear as a possibility only when one gets an 
insight into impermanence, suffering, and not-self."* Rather than running away from discomfort or trying to suppress it, the Thai Forest approach is to turn around and investigate suffering directly (*dukkha-sacca*). Notice that suffering is not a permanent fixture of the heart; it is a conditioned experience arising from attachment and craving (*taṇhā*). When observed with still, patient awareness, the knot of tension naturally unwinds.

The text observes: *"With his keen insight which was 
not blocked by any precious object (anàrammaõa§) he 
discovered that the pond of consciousness has the same crystal 
clear, lucid limpid nature it always had  for �the keen sighted."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.
